quests.hint: The vowel is long: it says the letter itself. Two vowel letters appear in the written word, but you only hear one vowel sound.
quests.explanation: A silent e after a single consonant makes the earlier vowel long: name, game, same. Without the e, you would read it as 'nam', with a short a.

quests.hint: It starts with the same digraph as 'shop' and has the long a of 'name'.
quests.explanation: The silent e works across the whole consonant that follows the vowel: shape, tape, grape. The digraph at the start doesn't change the pattern.

quests.hint: A sweet treat with a long a. Think back to how 'back' ends: this word ends differently.
quests.explanation: After a long vowel, the /k/ sound is a plain k, not ck: cake, take, bike. Save ck for after short vowels, as in back and clock.

quests.hint: Starts with a consonant pair, has a long i, and ends in a sound English won't leave bare at the end of a word.
quests.explanation: English words don't end in a plain v, so a silent e follows it: drive, give, have. Here the e also makes the i long, so it does two jobs.

quests.hint: One syllable. It sounds like 'tie' followed by the /m/ sound.
quests.explanation: The i…e pattern gives a long i across the m: time, line, mine. Compare 'Tim', which has a short i and no e.

quests.hint: A colour. Most speakers begin it with a simple /w/, but you need the same two-letter opening as in 'when'.
quests.explanation: The wh- spelling appears in question words and a few others: white, whale, wheel. Most speakers don't say the h, so it has to be memorised. The final e makes the i long.

quests.hint: It's where you live. The vowel is long o, and the e at the end stays silent.
quests.explanation: The o…e pattern gives a long o across the consonant: home, note, stone. The m is single, since a double m would make the vowel short.

quests.hint: The final e does two things at once: it makes the u say its own name, and it tells you how to say the g.
quests.explanation: The /dʒ/ sound needs a g before e, i or y, and English words almost never end in j. So huge ends in -ge, and the e also lengthens the u.

quests.hint: The opening /f/ sound is not written with f. The rest follows the same long-o pattern as 'home'.
quests.explanation: The letters ph make /f/ in words with Greek roots: phone, photo, graph. The word phone comes from the Greek for 'sound', which is why it isn't spelled with f.

quests.hint: The opposite of dirty. The long e is written with the two-vowel team that has an a in it.
quests.explanation: The sound /iː/ has several common spellings, including ea (clean, team) and ee (green, week). There is no rule for which one a word uses, so each word has to be learned with its spelling.

quests.hint: What you do in bed. The long e is spelled with two identical letters.
quests.explanation: The ee team is the most reliable spelling of /iː/ in the middle of short words: sleep, need, keep. Both e's are pronounced together as one long sound.

quests.hint: It begins with the consonant pair from 'plan'. Its ending sounds like /z/ but isn't written with z.
quests.explanation: Words with a long vowel team and a final /z/ often end in -se, not -s: please, cheese, tease. Without the e, the word would look like a plural (pleas).

quests.hint: White and cold, falling in winter. The long o comes at the end.
quests.explanation: At the end of a word, long o is often ow: snow, low, show. It follows the same idea as ay in 'day': the end of a word has its own spelling.

quests.hint: You wear it when it's cold. The long o sits between two consonants.
quests.explanation: Inside a syllable, /əʊ/ is often spelled oa: coat, boat, road. The oa team rarely ends a word, so it appears in the middle.

quests.hint: Two syllables. The first ends in a nasal-plus-d cluster, and the last sound is spelled with the same team as in 'snow'.
quests.explanation: The ow spelling keeps the final /əʊ/ sound: window, shadow, yellow. Say it slowly: win-dow. Both syllables use short, plain spellings.

quests.hint: Animals live here. The vowel sound is the open /ɑː/ you make at the doctor's.
quests.explanation: The letters ar make /ɑː/: farm, park, hard. When a vowel is followed by r, the r changes the vowel's sound, so this is not the same as the short a in 'cat'.

quests.hint: Thunder and rain. It opens with the consonant pair from 'stop' and closes on /m/.
quests.explanation: The letters or make /ɔː/: storm, fork, corn. Compare with ar in farm: the vowel letter is your only clue to the sound.

quests.hint: The first part of the day. Two syllables, and the second one is a plain ending you already know.
quests.explanation: The base is morn (the 'or' makes /ɔː/), and -ing is added with no change. Both n's stay: one ends morn, one begins -ing.

quests.hint: To change direction. The vowel sound is /ɜː/, and it isn't spelled with er or ir here.
quests.explanation: The sound /ɜː/ has three common spellings: ur (turn, hurt), ir (bird, first) and er (her, term). No rule predicts which one a word uses, so learn each word as a whole.

quests.hint: A human being. The stressed vowel sound is the same /ɜː/, and the spelling is the one in 'her'.
quests.explanation: Here /ɜː/ is written er: person, verb, serve. The second syllable, -son, is unstressed and sounds like /sən/, but it is written son.

quests.hint: A small animal that flies. The vowel is the same /ɜː/ sound, spelled with a different pair than in 'turn'.
quests.explanation: The ir spelling covers /ɜː/ in bird, girl, first, shirt. It comes up mostly in one-syllable words, but the spelling has to be memorised anyway.

quests.hint: It surrounds a garden. The /s/ sound is written with a letter that usually sounds like /k/, and there is a nasal sound before it.
quests.explanation: The letter c sounds like /s/ before e, i or y: fence, face, city. The ending -ence is common in words like silence and absence.

quests.hint: Bigger than a town. It begins with /s/, but the first letter is not s.
quests.explanation: C followed by i is soft: city, cinema, circle. If you began with s you would get 'sity', which is a plausible misspelling. The ending -ty is a common noun suffix.

quests.hint: You write with it. The middle sound is a soft c before an i, and the word ends with a quick /l/ syllable.
quests.explanation: Split it pen-cil. The c is soft before i, and the unstressed last syllable sounds like /sl/, but is written -cil, with an i you don't clearly hear.

quests.hint: A very tall person in a fairy tale. The first sound is /dʒ/, but g is enough to make it, if the next letter is right.
quests.explanation: Soft g before i or e is common (giant, gentle, magic), but not universal: gift, girl and give keep a hard g. Learn the exceptions as you meet them.

quests.hint: One side of a book. It ends with /dʒ/, and the vowel before it is long.
quests.explanation: English words almost never end in j, so the /dʒ/ sound at the end of a word is written -ge after a long vowel: page, cage, huge. Compare bridge, where a short vowel calls for -dge.

quests.hint: A trick performed with a wand. Two syllables, and both soft and hard sounds sit in the same word.
quests.explanation: Split it mag-ic. The g is soft before i (/dʒ/), and the final /k/ is written c, not k. The ending -ic is common in adjectives such as classic and basic.

quests.hint: Feeling good. Two syllables, and the middle sound follows a short vowel.
quests.explanation: A short vowel followed by a single consonant and then another syllable often doubles that consonant: happy, sunny, funny. The double letter protects the short vowel from turning long.

quests.hint: The opposite of outside. It is built from two words that you can already spell.
quests.explanation: Two parts, in + side, joined with no changes. The i…e pattern in the second half makes the long i, exactly as in 'time' and 'drive'.

quests.hint: You eat dinner at it. The first syllable has a long a, and the second has a consonant, a hidden vowel and a silent letter.
quests.explanation: Many words end in a consonant plus -le: table, little, apple. The last syllable sounds like /bəl/, but the vowel is never written as a separate letter before the l.
